rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's providence made livestock suit human financial needs and made them docile; without His will they would be neither useful nor manageable, unlike animals that remain burdensome.
rows.anchor: Had God not intended, neither would these beasts have been conducive to man’s needs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among the livestock, some serve as transport and others as food for people.
rows.anchor: some which are used by man as a means of transport and others which he uses as fodder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Livestock offer further benefits in their hides, hair, bones, dung and milk products, which are useful, delicious, healthy and nutritious.
rows.anchor: besides providing transport and fodder they also provide many other benefits: their hides, their hair, their bones and their faeces

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These benefits obligate people to show gratitude and obey the God who bestowed them.
rows.anchor: show gratitude and be obedient to the God who has bestowed these favours on them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessings and the Qur’an convey the same clear message, yet people evade it by dismissing the Qur’an as poetry instead of understanding and believing it.
rows.anchor: why are people trying to evade the Qur’ān by regarding it to be poetry instead of understanding and believing in such a clear fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Instead of recognizing their duties to God, the Quraysh invented idols and hoped ritual service to them would help them escape divine punishment.
rows.anchor: invented some false idols and by ritually serving these idols think that if ever God seizes them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols cannot help their worshippers; they too will be brought before God as accomplices, and He will determine the punishment.
rows.anchor: not be able to help these people in the slightest way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reassures the Prophet: he should bear the Quraysh’s insults, since God knows their secret plots and public words, and continue his mission trusting God to deal with his enemies.
rows.anchor: Let them call him by whatever names like poet, madman and fabricator they want to call him with.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The generic word “man” refers here to the Quraysh under discussion.
rows.anchor: The word ُانَنسِإِ signify the Quraysh who are under discussion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using the general term “man” expresses the author’s disgust with the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: This general word is used to express disgust.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍaraba mathalan can mean citing an example or wise saying, or speaking sarcastically and mocking; the mocking sense is intended here.
rows.anchor: Here this latter meaning is implied.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses continue the assurance in verse 76: arrogant Quraysh rival God, forget their creation and mock resurrection, just as they insult the Prophet.
rows.anchor: These verses are connected to those before them through two aspects: It relates to the assurance sounded to the Prophet (sws) in the previous verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier account of providence also leads to accountability: God’s favors entail gratitude and monotheism as well as a day of reward and punishment, which people evade.
rows.anchor: providence entails gratitude and believing in one God, it also entails a day of reward and punishment.

words: قُلْ يُحْيِيهَا ٱلَّذِىٓ أَنشَأَهَآ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who gave people life the first time will resurrect them; if their first creation was no burden for God, re-creation cannot be burdensome.
rows.anchor: the one who gave them life the first time will raise them to life again.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgetting one’s creation explains the foolish resurrection question: anyone remembering that God created him from clay would not ask it; asking makes him God’s rival.
rows.anchor: He who remembers that God created him from clay will never ask such a question.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here khalq means creatures: God is aware of all His creatures.
rows.anchor: In other words, God is aware of all His creatures.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge includes every part of people’s bodies, even after death: 67:14 says the Creator knows what He made, and 50:4 says what earth consumes is recorded with Him.
rows.anchor: He is aware of every bit and part of their body.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should not find resurrection from ashes and clay improbable when they see opposed elements produce one another; God brings fire from a lush green tree.
rows.anchor: By striking two branches of a lush green tree they create fire.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The green tree refers to trees found in some parts of Arabia, which desert travellers used as firestones.
rows.anchor: those who travel through deserts use them as firestone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier scholars offered another interpretation of the green-tree verse, but Islahi considers it far-fetched and prefers the explanation above.
rows.anchor: Some of our earlier scholars have interpreted this verse differently; however, I find it to be far-fetched.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disappearance of the Arabian trees does not weaken the argument: God causes things to become extinct, and the reasoning remains apt if the Qur’an’s first audience knew these trees.
rows.anchor: If today these trees do not exist or rarely exist, then this does not matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The underlying proof is that the world repeatedly shows opposing elements emerging from opposing elements, an established fact no one can dispute; even the greatest fire is found in water.
rows.anchor: The real basis of this reasoning is that examples of opposing elements coming into being from opposing elements exist in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God created the heavens and earth without difficulty, He can create people like them; people should compare which task is harder.
rows.anchor: They should think which is the more difficult of the two tasks.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attributes “supreme Creator” and “all-knowing” substantiate the premise more forcefully than 36:79: God has not tired or lost creative power and knows every creature’s components for reassembly.
rows.anchor: Here precisely the same thing is said in much more powerful words.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs no factories, investment, raw materials or machines to fulfill an intention; when He wills something, a directive is enough for it to materialize.
rows.anchor: God does not need anything to implement His intentions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Malakut means authority and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: means “authority and sovereignty.” Here at the end, the addressees of the sūrah are warned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God sovereignly controls everything and is free of defect, people should exalt Him; no partner shares His being, attributes or rights.
rows.anchor: No one is His partner in His being, attributes or rights. He is beyond and above any form of association.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God did not create the world without purpose; everyone must return to Him and answer for their deeds.
rows.anchor: He has not created this world without a purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Resurrecting people is easy for God, whose power covers everything and whose knowledge and observation encompass every word and deed.
rows.anchor: It is not the least difficult for Him to create people again once they die and decay

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like the previous sūrahs in this group, Ṣād is founded on tawḥīd; Quraysh oppose its reminder from arrogance and polytheism and will believe only when it is too late.
rows.anchor: Like the previous sūrahs of this group, this sūrah is also based on tawh@īd.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–11 present the Qur’an as a reminder rejected from arrogance, paralleling earlier nations; Quraysh too will believe only after seeing their fate, when faith is useless.
rows.anchor: This Qur’ān is a reminder for people; however, because of arrogance and haughtiness they are opposing it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh cannot accept a messenger from among themselves, so they call him sorcerer and liar; their leaders rally people to defend idols and ancestral religion.
rows.anchor: They are not able to digest the fact that a person from among them, as God’s messenger, should warn them of the fate of polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh imagine revelation should go to a wealthy notable and act as if they control the heavens and earth, unaware they will be helpless when God seizes them.
rows.anchor: For this reason, they are infatuated with the notion that had God intended to reveal a Book it would have been to some rich person among them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier peoples who arrogantly rejected God’s messengers met a terrible end; this history warns Quraysh not to invite God’s wrath, which they could not bear.
rows.anchor: Some previous nations are mentioned who had similarly adopted an arrogant attitude with regard to the messengers of God and ultimately met a horrible fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David’s hardships and power model patience: despite majesty he remained grateful and penitent, learned from others’ errors, and governed justly without arrogance or disorder.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is urged to be patient and steadfast. Some incidents from the life of David (sws) are referred to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning that the world is not amusement grounds belief in the Hereafter: otherwise reformers and wrongdoers would be equal, an unthinkable outcome for a wise Creator; the Qur’an calls people to reflect.
rows.anchor: this world is not a place of amusement. Those who regard this to be so disbelieve in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Solomon’s wealth and majesty, and his grateful, penitent response, serves the same purpose as the earlier account of David.
rows.anchor: The wealth and majesty of Solomon (sws) are mentioned and certain incidents relating to his grateful and penitent attitude are referred to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other prophets are briefly recalled to assure the Prophet: they endured hardship with fortitude and God granted them success in this world and the next.
rows.anchor: In order to assure the Prophet (sws) some other prophets of God are briefly alluded to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This world does not leave people unaccountable; a Judgment Day must come to reward the pious and punish wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: It is stated that this world is not a place in which people will be left unaccountable for their deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section has the Prophet declare that he is a warner, God alone is dominant, and the warning will come to pass; arrogant deniers follow Satan and will share his fate.
rows.anchor: a declaration is made by the Prophet (sws) that he is a warner and that there is no god except the one and dominant God
